## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Soṇanandajātaka* (Ja 532) is assigned to the *Sattatinipāta* of the Jātaka collection [Morris 1882; Fausböll 1891]. According to the traditional framing narrative, the Buddha recounted the story at Jetavana regarding a monk who supported his mother, remarking that wise persons in antiquity had likewise spurned universal rule over India to sustain their parents. In the story of the past, set in Benares when the city was known as Brahmavaddhana [Law 1926; Fausböll 1887], a royal family consisting of a king, queen, and two sons renounces worldly life for ascetic practice in the Himālayas [Anandajoti 2010]. The elder brother, the Bodhisatta named Soṇa (Soṇapaṇḍita), instructs his younger brother Nanda on the duties of filial care, paying exceptional attention to the virtue and veneration owed to one's mother [Anandajoti 2010; Ohnuma 2012]. The narrative also incorporates an episode detailing an encounter between King Manoja of Benares and the king of Kośala [Law 1926]. In the identification of the birth (*samodhāna*), Nanda is identified as Ānanda, King Manoja as Sāriputta, and Soṇa as the Bodhisatta [Fausböll 1891].
